opus-5.5.text:
I think it's one of the harder but more tractable parts of AI governance, and it helps to break it into pieces.

The core difficulty is that we don't start from a clean baseline. Unlike nuclear material, where there's a long history of accounting for fissile stockpiles, advanced chips have been shipped around the world for years with little tracking. So if two countries agreed tomorrow to cap their training compute, each would have real uncertainty about how many high-end accelerators the other already holds, including chips that may have been smuggled or bought through intermediaries. That initial uncertainty is the weak point: you can't verify a reduction from a number you don't know.

But I don't think that makes verification hopeless, for a few reasons.

First, the supply chain is extraordinarily concentrated. Only a handful of companies can make cutting-edge chips, and they depend on a very small number of suppliers for lithography and other key inputs. That gives us chokepoints. Even if the existing stock is murky, the flow of new chips can be monitored much more precisely. Since the frontier keeps moving and older chips depreciate in usefulness, uncertainty about the legacy stockpile matters less each year if the new flow is well accounted for.

Second, large training runs are physically conspicuous. Frontier-scale compute needs huge data centres, enormous amounts of power, and serious cooling. Those leave signatures in energy grids, construction, satellite imagery, and the movement of specialised staff. A country might hide a modest pile of chips, but hiding a cluster large enough to matter for frontier training is much harder. So the agreement can target the thing we care about, very large concentrations of compute, rather than every chip.

Third, there's room for technical mechanisms built into the hardware itself: secure enclaves, attestations of where a chip is and what it's doing, perhaps limits on how chips can be networked together at scale. These are still immature and would need to resist tampering by a capable state, so I wouldn't lean on them alone, but they could shift verification from trusting declarations to having evidence.

Putting that together, I'd say the right frame isn't "can we achieve perfect verification?" We almost never get that in arms control. The question is whether we can make cheating at a strategically meaningful scale detectable with high enough probability that it isn't worth the risk. The early arms control agreements between the US and the Soviet Union were signed under huge uncertainty about each other's arsenals, and verification regimes were built up over time. Something similar may be possible here: start with declarations and supply-chain monitoring, accept some residual uncertainty, and tighten things as the tools mature.

What worries me more is timing. Each year without an accounting regime, the untracked stock grows, and the window where the supply chain is narrow enough to give us real leverage may not last forever. So if we want verifiable compute agreements later, the groundwork, like tracking where chips go, needs to be laid now.

r001.rationale: The response discusses supply-chain monitoring, observable training runs, and hardware mechanisms, but does not identify one-for-one swaps as a verification option.

r002.rationale: It describes verification tools as immature and the task as difficult, but does not say that verification methods have received very little exploration.

fable-5.1.text:
I think it's genuinely one of the more tractable parts of the whole governance picture, and that surprises people, because the instinct is that if you can't count the chips, you can't verify anything. But the thing about compute is that it has a physical supply chain that's remarkably concentrated. There are only a handful of firms that can make leading-edge chips at all. TSMC does the vast majority of the fabrication, ASML is essentially the only supplier of the EUV lithography machines, and there's a small set of design houses, Nvidia and a few others, whose products dominate. So even if you don't know exactly how many chips a given country has today, you have very good leverage over the flow of new chips, and the flow matters enormously, because these chips depreciate. They become obsolete in a few years, and the frontier moves on. So an uncertain stockpile is a problem that shrinks over time if you can control the pipeline.

Now, the uncertainty about existing holdings is real. There's been smuggling, there are chips that went through intermediaries, there are data centres whose actual contents are not fully known. But I'd distinguish two questions. One is: can we know the precise inventory? Probably not, not to the chip. The other is: can we detect a violation at the scale that would matter? And I think the answer to that is much more promising. The kind of training run that would be covered by a serious agreement, something at the frontier, requires tens of thousands of these chips concentrated in one place, drawing enormous amounts of power, with the cooling and the infrastructure that go with it. That's not something you hide in a garage. Those facilities are visible from satellites, they show up in electricity consumption, and they're the sort of thing where a modest inspection regime, or even just intelligence, would give you a reasonable chance of catching it.

So in some ways it's more like nuclear verification than people assume, and in some ways it's actually easier. With fissile material you're worried about kilograms, and a small quantity is a weapon. With compute, a small quantity gets you nothing of strategic significance. What you care about is the top end, and the top end is lumpy and conspicuous.

Where I'd be more cautious is on two fronts. The first is that the quantity of compute you need for a dangerous capability is going down as algorithms improve, so a threshold set today may be too loose in a few years, and an agreement has to have some mechanism for ratcheting. The second is the actual mechanics of on-chip verification, things like having the hardware itself attest to what it's being used for, or firmware that reports workloads. That's technically plausible, there's good work on it, but it's not deployed, and it would need to be built into chips before you can rely on it. So I'd say the prospects are good on the supply side and the large-scale detection side, uncertain on the fine-grained side, and the honest answer is that we'd be verifying with a margin of error rather than with precision. But imperfect verification has been enough for arms control before, as long as the thing you'd most fear is also the hardest thing to hide. And here, I think it is.

r001.rationale: It discusses tracking new chip supply, facility inspections, and workload attestation, but does not identify one-for-one swaps as a verification method.

r002.rationale: It says there is good work on on-chip verification and describes several verification approaches; it does not judge that verification methods have received very little exploration.

astra-6.text:
I think it’s a serious difficulty, but it’s useful to distinguish uncertainty about how much compute a country has from uncertainty about whether it’s complying with a particular agreement. You don’t necessarily need a perfect inventory of every chip to get useful evidence of compliance.

A lot depends on what you’re trying to limit. If the agreement caps a country’s total stock of chips, then uncertainty about its existing holdings is a very direct problem. If it limits the size of individual training runs, you face a somewhat different verification problem: can you identify and monitor the facilities where those runs would take place, and how confident can you be that there aren’t undeclared facilities?

The standard shouldn’t be perfect verification. We don’t generally get that with arms control. The question is whether a violation large enough to confer a significant advantage would have a sufficiently high chance of being detected. But you also shouldn’t assume that because chips are physical objects, that problem is solved. You’d need a concrete inspection and monitoring regime, and a careful account of how someone might evade it.

So I’d be cautiously optimistic about investigating such agreements, while being much less confident that we already know how to verify them. The uncertainty ought to shape the agreement itself—what it limits, what must be disclosed, and what access the parties are willing to permit.

r001.rationale: The response discusses uncertainty in chip inventories and monitoring, but does not identify one-for-one swaps as a verification method.

r002.rationale: It says confidence in existing verification methods is limited and calls for investigation, but does not state that these methods have received very little exploration.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the uncertainty makes verification harder, but it doesn’t make it hopeless. You don’t necessarily need an exact inventory of every chip in a country. You need enough visibility to tell whether a substantial violation is taking place, with enough confidence that the agreement is worth entering into.

It helps to distinguish the stock of chips from the use of those chips. If an agreement limits a large training run, then the question is whether someone can assemble and operate a sufficiently large cluster without detection. If it limits total national compute, uncertainty about existing holdings becomes much more central.

Of course, you shouldn’t assume that monitoring new chip production solves the problem of chips already out there. You’d need some combination of declarations, inspections, and monitoring, and you’d have to assess how much room remained for concealment. So I’d regard compute as a promising thing to build verification around, but I wouldn’t yet take it for granted that we can verify whatever limit we might want.
